Across the 2020–2026 period, the global average retail petrol price stood at $2.28 USD/liter, with diesel averaging $2.13 USD/liter and LPG at $1.71 USD/liter. Brent Crude oil, the primary international benchmark, averaged $106.69 USD/barrel over the same period, fluctuating between $47.97 and $130.00 USD/barrel.

The widest petrol price range across any single country-week was $0.01 – $6.78 USD/liter, reflecting vast global disparities in taxation, subsidies, and market structure.

Brent-to-Retail Correlation

The Pearson correlation between Brent Crude and retail petrol prices is 0.264, indicating a moderate-to-strong positive relationship. Diesel shows a correlation of 0.259, while LPG has a correlation of 0.263. This confirms that while global crude benchmarks are a significant driver of retail prices, domestic policy interventions (subsidies, taxes, price caps) create meaningful dispersion in pass-through rates.

Figure 2.1: Scatter plot of Brent Crude vs. retail fuel prices with linear trend lines. Each point represents one country-week observation.
Figure 2.2: Distribution of country-level Pearson correlations between Brent Crude and retail petrol prices. The vertical dashed line marks the global pooled correlation.

Crisis Period Analysis

COVID-19 Demand Shock (2020)
Brent Crude bottomed at $47.97 USD/bbl on Apr 27, 2020. Global average retail petrol fell to $1.02 USD/L — a 24.2% drop from pre-pandemic levels ($1.46 USD/L). The lag between crude and retail troughs was approximately 2–4 weeks. Takeaway: Retail prices followed crude down but with a visible lag, and the percentage decline at the pump was attenuated by fixed tax components.
2022 Energy Price Crisis
Brent Crude peaked at $130.00 USD/bbl on Mar 28, 2022. Global average retail petrol reached $2.78 USD/L — a 152.3% surge from the COVID trough. The pass-through from crude to retail was more immediate during the upward shock. Takeaway: Price increases transmitted faster than decreases, consistent with the "rockets and feathers" asymmetry documented in energy economics.
Figure 2.3: Side-by-side comparison of Brent Crude and average retail petrol during the COVID-19 shock (left) and the 2022 energy crisis (right).

Yearly Volatility

Weekly price volatility (measured as the standard deviation of percentage changes) was 1.55% for petrol and 1.54% for Brent Crude. Retail volatility consistently trailed crude volatility, suggesting that downstream price rigidities — whether from regulation or market structure — partially dampened crude swings before they reached consumers.

Figure 2.4: Yearly cross-country standard deviation of retail fuel prices, a measure of dispersion and volatility across the 84-country sample.

Price Stability by Income Level

Price stability — measured by the cross-country standard deviation within each income group — reveals whether countries at similar income levels experience similar price dynamics. Low-income countries show the highest year-to-year volatility variation, reflecting weaker institutional capacity for price stabilization.

Figure 5.3: Yearly petrol price standard deviation within each income group, a measure of intra-group price dispersion and instability.
Tax-to-Price Ratio by Income Level:
High-income countries impose an average tax rate of 34.7% on petrol, compared to 21.1% for middle-income and 22.9% for low-income countries. Takeaway: The tax burden gap between high- and low-income countries (11.9 percentage points) reflects fundamentally different fiscal approaches to fuel — high-income nations use fuel taxes as revenue instruments, while low-income nations often suppress taxes to maintain affordability.

6. Key Findings & Policy Implications

Synthesize the most important insights into actionable findings with recommendations for policymakers on subsidy design, tax calibration, and price stabilization mechanisms.

Finding 1: Brent Crude explains a significant but incomplete share of retail price variation.
The global Brent-to-petrol correlation is r = 0.264. While crude movements are the dominant cost driver, domestic policy (subsidies, taxes, price caps) and market structure create substantial country-level deviations. Country-level correlations range widely, confirming that policy interventions materially alter the crude-to-retail transmission. Policy implication: Countries cannot rely on crude price stabilization alone; domestic policy levers are essential for managing consumer-level price outcomes.
Finding 2: Subsidies deliver measurable price dampening, but the effect varies dramatically by income level.
High/Very High subsidy countries pay 86.8% less on average for petrol than low-subsidy countries. However, the dampening effect is 83.9% for low-income countries vs. 90.1% for high-income countries, reflecting the fiscal constraints low-income governments face in sustaining subsidies. Policy implication: Subsidy design must account for fiscal sustainability. Low-income countries may need international financing mechanisms to maintain effective subsidy programs during price shocks.
Finding 3: Price pass-through from crude to retail is lower in high-subsidy regimes.
The Brent–petrol correlation for Very High subsidy countries (0.306) is lower than for Low subsidy countries (0.554), confirming that subsidies buffer consumers from global crude swings — but at growing fiscal cost during prolonged high-price periods. Policy implication: Subsidies are effective shock absorbers but become fiscally unsustainable during extended price spikes. Automatic stabilization mechanisms (e.g., variable subsidies that phase out as prices normalize) can balance protection and fiscal discipline.
Finding 4: Regional price inequality peaked during the 2022 crisis.
The regional petrol price spread reached $2.87/liter in 2026, as crude price shocks amplified pre-existing structural differences in taxation and subsidy regimes. Regions with minimal fiscal buffers saw the steepest retail price increases. Policy implication: International coordination on strategic petroleum reserves and cross-subsidy mechanisms could reduce regional price inequality during future shocks.
Finding 5: Asymmetric price transmission — "rockets and feathers" — is evident in the data.
During the 2022 energy crisis, retail prices rose sharply and quickly in response to Brent increases. During the 2020 COVID collapse, retail prices declined more slowly and incompletely, with a 2–4 week lag to trough. This asymmetry disadvantages consumers and warrants regulatory attention. Policy implication: Price monitoring agencies should track pass-through speed in both directions. Regulatory mechanisms that enforce symmetric price adjustment could protect consumers from systematic overcharging during downward crude movements.
Finding 6: The tax burden gap between high- and low-income countries is 11.9 percentage points.
High-income countries average 34.7% tax on petrol, while low-income countries average 22.9%. This gap reflects a trade-off: high taxes fund public budgets but raise consumer costs; low taxes improve affordability but reduce fiscal space for other priorities. Policy implication: Progressive tax calibration — where fuel taxes fund targeted social transfers — can reconcile revenue needs with equity. Low-income countries should explore revenue-neutral tax reforms that shift the fuel tax burden toward higher-income consumers.

Summary of Policy Recommendations

#RecommendationRationale
1Implement automatic subsidy stabilization mechanismsBuffers during shocks, phases out during calm — avoids fiscal unsustainability
2Establish symmetric pass-through monitoringAddresses "rockets and feathers" asymmetry that systematically disadvantages consumers
3Develop international financing for low-income country subsidiesLow-income countries lack fiscal space for effective subsidies; multilateral support is needed
